events.title: The coronation of Mary I
events.shortBlurb: Crowned at Westminster by the Bishop of Winchester, Mary Tudor became the first queen of England anointed in her own right…
body: When Edward VI died on 6 July 1553, the Duke of Northumberland's devise set aside the king's half-sisters for Lady Jane Grey, proclaimed on 10 July. The country would not have her; within nine days Mary's cause had prevailed, and on 3 August she entered London in triumph.

On Sunday 1 October 1553 she was crowned in Westminster Abbey by Stephen Gardiner, Bishop of Winchester — the Archbishop of Canterbury being a prisoner in the Tower. It was done, the old account notes, in spite of the excommunication that still lay upon the country; the conduits at Cornhill and Cheapside ran with wine.

She was the first woman anointed queen of England in her own right. Within two years Parliament had restored the old worship and received Cardinal Pole as legate, reconciling the realm to the Apostolic See. The restoration lasted barely five years, and is remembered more for the fires of Smithfield than for the coronation pomp.
